title: MODULE 02 — Semantic HTML and Modern Document Engineering

overview.text: This module builds directly on Module 01. Students have learned how browsers retrieve and render webpages; now they will learn how to construct the actual documents that browsers process.

The focus is not simply memorizing HTML tags. It is learning how to build structured, meaningful, accessible, search-engine-friendly web documents that can serve as the foundation for professional frontend applications.
Master the foundation of every web interface.
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to structure content on the web. It defines the meaning and organization of documents that browsers interpret and display.

Professional frontend development requires more than knowing individual HTML elements. Developers must understand document structure, semantic meaning, navigation architecture, multimedia integration, forms, validation, structured data, search engine metadata, and accessibility.

This module develops the ability to engineer complete, well-structured HTML documents that can be styled with CSS, enhanced with JavaScript, accessed by assistive technologies, and understood by search engines.
By the end of this module, students should be able to:

items: Construct valid HTML5 documents using appropriate document structure and elements.
Understand elements, attributes, nesting, document metadata, and HTML parsing.
Use semantic HTML elements to communicate the purpose of different content regions.
Organize content using headings, paragraphs, lists, and appropriate document hierarchy.
Design internal and external navigation using links and meaningful URL structures.
Integrate images, audio, video, and embedded resources.
Build accessible forms using appropriate input types and controls.
Implement native HTML form validation and the Constraint Validation API.
Represent structured information using accessible HTML tables.
Configure metadata, Open Graph information, and fundamental SEO elements.
Apply accessibility principles using semantic HTML and native browser behavior.
Build a complete multi-page website using reusable document structures.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — HTML Document Structure and Elements

blocks.text: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
It is the standard markup language used to define the structure and meaning of web documents.
HTML tells the browser what different pieces of content represent.

items: A heading represents a title or heading.
A paragraph represents a block of text.
A link represents navigation to another resource.
A form represents a user-input mechanism.
A table represents structured tabular information.

blocks.text: HTML does not primarily control the visual appearance of a website. That responsibility belongs to CSS.
JavaScript adds interactive behavior and dynamic functionality.
**CSS:** Defines presentation, layout, and visual appearance.
**JavaScript:** Defines interactive behavior and dynamic operations.
An HTML element generally consists of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.

items: `This is a paragraph.` is the text content.
The complete structure is the paragraph element.

blocks.text: HTML elements describe how the browser and other tools should interpret the content.
These three terms are related but have different meanings.
A tag is the markup syntax used to identify an element.
An element is the complete structure represented by its tags, content, and applicable attributes.
An attribute provides additional information or configuration for an element.
Every standard HTML document should have an appropriate document structure.

The DOCTYPE declaration tells the browser to interpret the document using modern HTML standards mode rather than legacy quirks mode.
It is not an HTML element.
The `html` element is the root element of the document.
The `lang` attribute identifies the primary language of the document.
This helps browsers, search engines, translation tools, and assistive technologies interpret the content.
The `head` element contains document metadata and references to resources such as stylesheets and icons.
It generally contains information that is not displayed as the main page content.
The `body` element contains the document's actual content.
Most visible webpage elements belong inside the body.
1.5 Understanding Void Elements and Normal Elements
Most HTML elements have opening and closing tags.
However, some elements are void elements. They cannot contain child content and do not have closing tags.
A normal element can contain text, other elements, or both.
HTML elements can contain other elements.

Always understand the HTML content model and the elements permitted inside other elements.
Global attributes can be used on many HTML elements.
Provides a unique identifier within a document.
Provides one or more class names, often used by CSS and JavaScript.
Provides advisory information, commonly presented as a tooltip by some browsers.
Do not rely on `title` alone to communicate essential instructions or information.
Indicates that an element is not currently relevant for presentation.
JavaScript can access this information through `dataset`.

Home Courses
Comments are not displayed as normal page content.
They can help developers organize complex documents, but excessive comments that simply repeat obvious code should be avoided.
Some characters have special meaning in HTML.
For example, `<` and `>` are used to construct tags.
HTML character references allow these characters to be displayed as text.
HTML also supports numeric character references for representing Unicode characters.
The browser does not simply display HTML source code.
It parses the document and constructs a DOM according to HTML parsing rules.
This means invalid markup may be corrected or rearranged during parsing.
For frontend developers, this has an important consequence:
The DOM visible in browser developer tools may not exactly match the original source code.
Understanding this behavior helps prevent problems caused by incorrect nesting, omitted structural elements, and invalid markup.

sections.title: LESSON 02 — Semantic HTML and Document Outline

blocks.text: Semantic HTML means using HTML elements according to the meaning and purpose of their content.
A semantic element describes what its content represents rather than merely how it should look.
Both structures can be styled to look similar.
However, the second communicates the purpose of its elements directly through HTML semantics.
Semantic elements communicate a particular meaning or purpose.
Non-semantic elements generally do not communicate a particular content role.
Non-semantic elements are still important. They should be used when no more suitable semantic element exists, or when a generic container is necessary for styling and application behavior.
Do not force semantic elements into places where their meaning does not fit.
The `header` element represents introductory content or navigational assistance for its nearest relevant sectioning context.
A page may contain more than one header, such as a page header and an article header.
The `nav` element represents a major group of navigation links.
Use `nav` for major navigation, not for every random group of links.
The `main` element represents the dominant content of the document.
A normal document should have one main content landmark.
The `section` element represents a thematic grouping of content.

Popular Courses

Explore our most popular learning programmes.
A section will generally have a heading that identifies its topic.
Do not use `section` simply because you need a generic styling container. Use `div` when no semantic grouping is intended.
The `article` element represents a self-contained composition that could make sense independently.

Introduction to HTML

HTML provides the structure of web documents.

Read article
The `aside` element represents content that is indirectly related to the surrounding content.
The `footer` element represents footer information for its nearest relevant sectioning context or the page.
A well-organized document separates content according to its meaning.

A document outline is the conceptual hierarchy of information within a document.
For a website, the structure may look like:

Frontend Engineering

├── Introduction
│   ├── What Is Frontend Engineering?

The heading elements should communicate this hierarchy.

items: `h4`, `h5`, and `h6` identify progressively deeper content levels.

blocks.text: The document's structure should be meaningful even when the CSS is disabled.

An important implementation detail: do not rely on a theoretical automatic HTML document-outline algorithm to reorganize headings. Modern browsers and assistive technologies use explicit heading levels. Authors must deliberately create a sensible heading hierarchy.
Semantic elements provide built-in meaning and browser behavior.
A real button supports keyboard interaction, focus behavior, and button semantics.
The `div` does not automatically behave like a keyboard-accessible button.
To make it function equivalently, developers would have to recreate many behaviors manually.
Prefer native semantic elements whenever possible.

items: Using headings only to make text visually large.
Skipping heading levels without a meaningful structural reason.
Using `section` as a generic replacement for every `div`.
Using `article` for content that is not independently meaningful.
Using `nav` around every group of links.
Using semantic elements purely for visual styling.
Adding ARIA roles to elements that already provide the required native semantics.

sections.title: LESSON 04 — Links, Navigation and Internal Page Architecture

blocks.text: Links allow users to navigate between documents and resources.
The `a` element, also known as the anchor element, creates a hyperlink.
Links are fundamental to the interconnected structure of the web.
An absolute URL contains the complete resource address.
Use absolute URLs when linking to external websites or when a complete address is required.
A relative URL identifies a resource based on the current document's URL.

website/
│
├── index.html
├── courses.html
├── about.html
│
└── pages/
    ├── contact.html
    └── privacy.html
To access a file inside the pages directory:
From `pages/contact.html`, you can move back to the root:
The `..` segment represents the parent directory in a relative URL path.
A root-relative path begins at the website's URL root.
It is useful when a website has a consistent root structure.
However, developers deploying an application under a subdirectory must consider the hosting configuration and base path.
A webpage can link to a particular section using an element's `id`.

Browser behavior depends on the resource, origin, response headers, and supported browser features.

Breadcrumbs are particularly useful for content-heavy websites, documentation platforms, and large learning platforms.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — Images, Audio, Video and Embedded Content

blocks.text: Modern websites use multimedia to communicate information and provide interactive experiences.
HTML supports several native elements for embedding media:
Understanding these elements is necessary for building accessible, responsive, and performant interfaces.
The `img` element embeds an image into a document.
Provides alternative text for users who cannot see the image.
Describe the image's intrinsic dimensions in CSS pixels and help browsers reserve layout space.
Controls loading behavior, such as eager or lazy loading.
Alternative text is one of the most important aspects of image accessibility.
For informative images, write meaningful descriptions of the information the image communicates.
For decorative images that do not add meaningful information, use an empty alternative text value:
This prevents unnecessary announcements by assistive technologies.
Avoid using filenames as alternative text.
Alternative text should convey the image's relevant purpose, not describe every visible detail regardless of context.
Specifying image dimensions helps prevent unexpected layout shifts during loading.
The browser can scale the image while maintaining its aspect ratio.
Lazy loading delays the loading of certain images until they approach the visible area.
This can reduce initial page-loading work on long pages.
However, do not automatically lazy-load every image.
Important above-the-fold images, particularly a prominent hero image, may need eager loading to avoid delaying the largest visible content.
5.6 Responsive Images With srcset and sizes
Different devices may need different image sizes.
The `srcset` attribute allows developers to offer multiple image resources.
The browser uses the available information and device conditions to select an appropriate image resource.
This is useful when serving large content images to desktop users and smaller versions to mobile users.
The `picture` element provides more control over image resource selection.
It can also be used for art direction and modern image formats with appropriate fallback resources.
The `figure` element represents self-contained content such as an image, diagram, chart, or code example.
The `figcaption` element provides a caption for that figure.
This clearly connects the image with its explanation.

<audio controls>
    <source src="lesson.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
    <source src="lesson.ogg" type="audio/ogg">

    Your browser does not support HTML audio.
</audio>
The `controls` attribute enables the browser's native audio controls.
Autoplay behavior is restricted by browsers and should not be relied upon.
For prerecorded audio information, provide a transcript when appropriate.

<video
    controls
    width="800"
    height="450"
    poster="video-thumbnail.jpg"
>
    <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <source src="lesson.webm" type="video/webm">

    Your browser does not support HTML video.
</video>
The `poster` attribute identifies a preview image shown before playback.
The `track` element provides timed text tracks associated with audio and video.

<video controls width="800">
    <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">

    <track
        kind="captions"
        src="lesson-en.vtt"
        srclang="en"
        label="English"
        default
    >
</video>
Captions are particularly important for deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
Text alternatives and transcripts can also benefit users in environments where sound is unavailable.
The `iframe` element embeds another browsing context inside the current document.

<iframe
    src="https://example.com"
    title="Example website preview"
    width="800"
    height="500"
    loading="lazy"
>
</iframe>
Embedded content can introduce security and privacy concerns.
Provides an accessible name describing the embedded content.
Restricts capabilities available to the embedded content.

<iframe
    src="https://example.com"
    title="External application"
    sandbox
    width="800"
    height="500"
>
</iframe>
Additional sandbox permissions may be granted only when necessary.
Can restrict or grant specified browser capabilities through Permissions Policy.
Controls which referrer information is sent when requesting the embedded resource.
Do not grant broad iframe permissions without understanding why the embedded content needs them.
Some embedded sites also restrict framing through HTTP security headers, so an iframe will not necessarily work for every external URL.
Large images and media files can significantly affect page performance.

items: Use modern image formats when suitable.
Use lazy loading for appropriate below-the-fold images.
Avoid autoplaying large media without a clear need.
Provide captions and transcripts where appropriate.
Use media hosting or CDN infrastructure when suitable.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — HTML Forms and Input Types

blocks.text: Forms allow users to provide information to a website.
The `form` element provides the structure for collecting and submitting user input.

<form action="/register" method="post">

    <label for="name">Full Name</label>

    <input
        type="text"
        id="name"
        name="name"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">
        Register
    </button>

</form>
Defines the URL to which the form submission is directed.
Defines the HTTP method used for submission.
Describes a form control for users and assistive technologies.
Defines the form field's submission name.
Defines the behavior and expected input type.
Specifies that a control must be completed before successful native form submission.
HTML forms commonly use GET or POST.

<form action="/search" method="get">

    <label for="query">Search Courses</label>

    <input
        type="search"
        id="query"
        name="q"
    >

    <button type="submit">Search</button>

</form>
The submitted form values are generally encoded into the URL query string.
GET is appropriate for requests that retrieve information and whose parameters can be represented in the URL.

items: Parameters may appear in browser history and logs.
GET should not be used to perform operations that change server state.

blocks.text:
<form action="/register" method="post">

    <label for="email">Email Address</label>

    <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">Create Account</button>

</form>
POST submits the form data in the request body.
It is commonly used for operations that create or modify server-side information.
Important distinction: POST does not automatically encrypt data. HTTPS is still required to protect information in transit.
Every form control should have a suitable accessible label.
The explicit label association uses matching `for` and `id` values.
An alternative is an implicit label:
Labels improve usability because activating the label can focus or toggle the associated control.
Placeholder text is not a substitute for a label.
HTML provides multiple input types to match different data.
For email-address input and basic browser validation.
It does not prove that an address exists or belongs to the user.
The browser typically masks the displayed characters.
A phone input does not automatically establish one universal telephone-number format because formats vary internationally.
The number input accepts numerical values.

<label for="age">Age</label>

<input
    type="number"
    id="age"
    name="age"
    min="18"
    max="100"
>
The `min`, `max`, and `step` attributes can define constraints.
Use number inputs for quantities, not arbitrary digit-based identifiers such as phone numbers or postal codes.
HTML supports date and time-related controls.

<input type="date" name="date">

<input type="time" name="time">

<input type="datetime-local" name="appointment">

<input type="month" name="month">

<input type="week" name="week">
The displayed interface can differ between browsers and operating systems.
The submitted value follows the appropriate standardized format.
Checkboxes allow users to select independent options.

<fieldset>
    <legend>Select Learning Interests</legend>

    <label>
        <input
            type="checkbox"
            name="interests"
            value="frontend"
        >
        Frontend
    </label>

    <label>
        <input
            type="checkbox"
            name="interests"
            value="backend"
        >
        Backend
    </label>

    <label>
        <input
            type="checkbox"
            name="interests"
            value="data-engineering"
        >
        Data Engineering
    </label>

</fieldset>
Multiple checked controls with the same name may submit multiple values.
Radio buttons allow the user to select one option from a group.

<fieldset>

    <legend>Choose Your Experience Level</legend>

    <label>
        <input
            type="radio"
            name="level"
            value="beginner"
            required
        >
        Beginner
    </label>

    <label>
        <input
            type="radio"
            name="level"
            value="intermediate"
        >
        Intermediate
    </label>

    <label>
        <input
            type="radio"
            name="level"
            value="advanced"
        >
        Advanced
    </label>

</fieldset>
Radio controls belong to the same group when they share the same name in the applicable form owner and tree context.
A select control allows users to choose from a predefined list.

<label for="course">Select a Course</label>

<select id="course" name="course" required>

    <option value="">Choose a course</option>

    <option value="frontend">Frontend Engineering</option>

    <option value="backend">Backend Engineering</option>

    <option value="data">Data Engineering</option>

</select>
The `multiple` attribute allows selecting multiple options.
Use `optgroup` to organize larger option lists into logical groups.

<label for="message">Your Message</label>

<textarea
    id="message"
    name="message"
    rows="5"
    cols="40"
    placeholder="Write your message..."
></textarea>
Creates a general-purpose button without submitting the form by default.
Resets form controls to their initial values.
Be careful with reset buttons because they can unintentionally erase user-entered information.
Always specify the intended button type, especially inside forms.
Hidden inputs carry values that are not displayed as normal form fields.
Hidden input values are not trustworthy merely because users cannot see them.
Users can inspect and modify client-side form data. The server must validate submitted values and enforce authorization.
The file input allows users to select local files.

<form
    action="/upload"
    method="post"
    enctype="multipart/form-data"
>

    <label for="resume">Upload Resume</label>

    <input
        type="file"
        id="resume"
        name="resume"
        accept=".pdf"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">Upload</button>

</form>
When submitting files through a standard HTML form, `multipart/form-data` is generally required.
The `accept` attribute guides the file picker but is not a security boundary.
The backend must independently validate file type, size, content, and upload permissions.
The `legend` element provides a descriptive title for the group.

<fieldset>

    <legend>Personal Information</legend>

    <label for="first-name">First Name</label>
    <input
        type="text"
        id="first-name"
        name="firstName"
    >

    <label for="last-name">Last Name</label>
    <input
        type="text"
        id="last-name"
        name="lastName"
    >

</fieldset>
This is especially useful for large forms.
The `autocomplete` attribute tells the browser what type of information a field expects.

<input
    type="text"
    name="name"
    autocomplete="name"
>

<input
    type="email"
    name="email"
    autocomplete="email"
>

<input
    type="password"
    name="password"
    autocomplete="new-password"
>
For an existing password field, `current-password` may be more appropriate.
Good autocomplete configuration can make forms faster and easier to use.
Create a complete course registration form.

items: Every control must have an accessible label.
Group related inputs using fieldset and legend.
Use GET or POST according to the purpose of the form.
Include a clearly named submit button.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — Form Validation and Constraint Validation API

blocks.text: Form validation determines whether submitted information meets defined requirements.

items: Password must meet a minimum length.
Age must fall within an acceptable range.

blocks.text: Validation helps prevent incomplete or incorrectly formatted submissions.
There are two major layers to understand:
**Client-side validation:** Performed in the browser before form submission.
**Server-side validation:** Performed by the backend after receiving submitted information.
Client-side validation improves usability, but it must never be treated as a security boundary.
The `required` attribute prevents successful native form submission when the associated control is missing an appropriate value.

<form>

    <label for="email">Email</label>

    <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>

</form>
The browser checks that the field satisfies the applicable constraints before submission.
These attributes define minimum and maximum text lengths.
This requires the text to be within the specified length constraints.
Use these attributes to provide clear input boundaries.
For number and supported date-related inputs, `min` and `max` define value boundaries.
An out-of-range value will fail the corresponding native constraint.
The `step` attribute controls valid increments for applicable numerical and date-related controls.
The `pattern` attribute allows developers to define a regular-expression pattern for text-like input types that support it.

<label for="student-id">Student ID</label>

<input
    type="text"
    id="student-id"
    name="studentId"
    pattern="[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{4}"
    title="Enter two uppercase letters followed by four digits."
    required
>
The pattern must match the complete input value according to HTML pattern-matching rules.
Pattern validation should be clear and forgiving enough for legitimate input.
Do not invent restrictive patterns without understanding valid user data.
Certain input types provide built-in validation.
The browser can identify some malformed email formats.
However, browser validation does not establish:

items: Whether the user owns that address.
Whether the address can receive messages.

blocks.text: HTML provides a browser API for inspecting and controlling form validation.
Returns whether the control or form satisfies its constraints.
Checks constraints and asks the browser to display validation feedback when applicable.
Sets a custom validation message for a control.
An empty string clears the custom error.

<form id="registration-form">

    <label for="username">Username</label>

    <input
        type="text"
        id="username"
        name="username"
        minlength="3"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">Register</button>

</form>
The validity state provides more specific information about validation failures.
Suppose a registration form requires a username that must not contain spaces.

<label for="username">Username</label>

<input
    type="text"
    id="username"
    name="username"
    minlength="3"
    required
>
The custom validation message is set while the input is invalid and cleared when the issue is corrected.

<form id="register-form">

    <label for="email">Email</label>

    <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
    >

    <label for="password">Password</label>

    <input
        type="password"
        id="password"
        name="password"
        minlength="8"
        required
    >

    <button type="submit">Create Account</button>

</form>

sections.title: LESSON 09 — HTML Metadata, Open Graph and SEO Fundamentals

blocks.text: Metadata is information that describes a web document.
It is generally defined inside the document's `head` element.
Metadata helps browsers, search engines, and other services interpret a webpage.
The `meta charset` declaration identifies the document's character encoding.
UTF-8 is the standard recommended encoding for modern HTML documents.
It supports a broad range of international characters.
Place this declaration near the beginning of the document head.
This tells mobile browsers to use the device's viewport width when calculating the layout viewport.
Without suitable viewport configuration, mobile rendering may not behave as expected.
Do not unnecessarily disable user zoom because this can reduce accessibility.
The `title` element defines the document title.
The meta description provides a brief description of the page.

<meta
    name="description"
    content="Learn modern frontend engineering through structured lessons, practical examples, and projects."
>
Search engines may use the description when constructing search snippets, but they can choose other content instead.
A useful description should accurately explain the page and encourage relevant users to visit it.
The robots metadata can provide crawling and indexing instructions to participating search engines.
A page that should not be indexed might use:
The actual indexing behavior depends on crawler support, page accessibility, and applicable directives.
Do not accidentally deploy `noindex` on pages that should appear in search results.
Robots metadata is not an access-control or security mechanism.
A canonical link identifies the preferred URL for a page when multiple URLs may represent substantially identical content.
This can help search engines understand which URL should be treated as the preferred version.
Canonicalization should reflect the actual preferred URL.
It does not automatically redirect users or prevent duplicate content from being accessible.
A favicon provides a small visual identity for a website.
A modern site may also provide PNG, SVG, or other supported icon resources.
The available icon formats and behavior depend on browser and platform support.
Open Graph metadata helps describe a webpage when it is shared on supported social platforms and other services.

<meta property="og:type" content="website">

<meta
    property="og:title"
    content="Frontend Engineering Course | PrepSpaces"
>

    property="og:description"
    content="Learn frontend engineering through structured lessons and projects."
>

>

    property="og:image"
    content="https://prepspaces.com/images/frontend-course-preview.jpg"
>
The image should be publicly accessible and suitable for social sharing.

<meta
    name="twitter:card"
    content="summary_large_image"
>

    name="twitter:title"
    content="Frontend Engineering Course"
>

    name="twitter:description"

>

<meta
    name="twitter:image"
    content="https://prepspaces.com/images/frontend-course-preview.jpg"
>
The actual display depends on the platform's current support and processing behavior.
Social metadata should match the page content rather than presenting misleading information.
Search Engine Optimization (SEO) refers to improving a website's ability to be discovered and understood through search engines.
HTML contributes to SEO through several important practices.
Every important page should have an informative title.
Use a meaningful heading hierarchy to organize the content.
Use appropriate elements such as article, nav, main, and headings.
Use meaningful anchor text instead of generic labels such as "click here."
Create links that allow search engines and users to discover important pages.
Each important page should serve a clear purpose and provide content that satisfies its intended audience.
Make sure content works at different viewport sizes.
Structured data can provide machine-readable descriptions of information on a webpage.
For example, certain content types may support structured data represented using Schema.org vocabulary and JSON-LD.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Course",
  "name": "Frontend Engineering",
  "description": "A structured course covering modern frontend development."
}
</script>
Structured data must accurately represent visible page content and comply with applicable search engine guidelines.
Adding structured data does not guarantee enhanced search results.

After completing this module, students should be able to independently create a structured HTML website consisting of multiple connected pages.

They should understand when to use semantic elements, how to create meaningful content hierarchy, how to implement multimedia and accessible forms, how to use browser-native validation, and how to structure metadata for search engines and social sharing.
The expected outcome is the ability to write HTML that is not merely visually presentable, but also meaningful, maintainable, accessible, and suitable for real-world frontend applications.

**Course progression:** Module 01 taught how the browser and web infrastructure work. Module 02 now teaches how to engineer the documents the browser interprets. The next module can build on this structure with CSS without needing to repeat HTML fundamentals.
